To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the local charge distribution of acceptors in WS 2 single crystal can be directly imaged using scanning tunneling microscopy (STM).

the topographic depresssion and the ring structures in CITS measurements of acceptors in WS 2 are explained by two different current mechanisms, namely tunneling into the valence band and the conduction bands of WS 2, respectively, and that photoassisted STM measurements do not reveal a photoinduced enhancement of the minority charge carrier recombiantion at the acceptor sites.
the acceptors are ionized, and they are not recombination centers for minority carriers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a detailed characterization of acceptor sites in p-type WS _{2} single crystals.
the investigation of the local electronic and chemical properties of p-type WS ₂ single crystals.
the development of new concepts and methods for the investigation of dopant atoms in semiconductors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the observed topographic depressions are caused by an enhanced minority charge-carrier recombination at ionized acceptors.

the observed ring structure in CITS and the reduction of the LSPV in photoinduced tunnel spectroscopy measurements at acceptor sites are due to the local charge distribution and not due to a local enhancement of recombination.
the ring structures are caused by a lateral redistribution of the local potential due to an accumulation of minority charge carriers in the vicinity of acceptor sites.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have investigated the acceptor states in p-type WS _{2} by using different STM techniques.
the topographic depresses and the ring structures are caused by the local charge distribution of ionized acceptor dopants.
the acceptors are ionized and do not act as recombination centers.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the topographic depresssion and the ring structure observed by CITS are not directly linked to the acceptors but to the tip-induced band bending in the vicinity of these defects.
the ring structures observed by CITS are a consequence of an enhanced majority carrier tunneling current, which is not related to the acceptor states.
the ring structure in CITS measurements is not a signature of dopants but rather of local variations of the band bending.
